schools.summary: Gill restricts “all Israel” to the northern men already settled in Judah.
Henry rules out a political motive and reads the invitation as purely religious.
Clarke explains how a Judean proclamation could circulate in Israel at all; Wesley says why Ephraim and Manasseh are the two tribes named.
Ellicott treats the word for letters as a late Persian loan and dates the appeal by the regnal years of Hoshea.

debates.question: Who are the two audiences of the verse?

sides.position: “All Israel and Judah” means the people within Hezekiah’s own borders, northern men included
The letters to Ephraim and Manasseh address the northern kingdom proper

debates.question: How could a king of Judah proclaim a feast inside Israel?

sides.position: Hoshea was one of the best of their kings and did not forbid it
Both golden calves had by then been carried off by the Assyrians, so the rival shrines were gone
The regnal dates place this in Hoshea’s third year, and he did not actively oppose a national passover

outliers.note: He puts the distinction in the king’s own mouth — let them take whom they will for their king, so they will but take him for their God — and notes that Hezekiah sought the good of a kingdom that paid him no tribute and had lately vexed his own.

themes: Hezekiah sent to all Israel and Judah
1.pericope_label: Hezekiah sends to all Israel to keep the passover

schools.summary: Gill has the king consult his nobles with the great senate of the nation.
Keil and Delitzsch note that both legal grounds for postponement were present at once; Ellicott places the council before the fourteenth of Nisan and names the two months with their Assyrian forms.
Henry argues the case as a maxim about not losing the substance to a nicety of timing.
Clarke states the alternative — Ijar or a whole year’s delay — and leaves the lawfulness to the outcome; Wesley extends the individual proviso to the congregation.

debates.question: Who made the decision?

sides.position: The king with his nobles and the great senate of the nation
The community of the capital assembled in their representatives
The king determined it, in council with grandees and popular representatives, before the proper date had passed

debates.question: Was extending the proviso to the whole congregation lawful?

sides.position: The law provided for particular persons; he doubted not it might be stretched to the congregation
They thought it might be stretched because of the delay the cleansing imposed, and the result showed they had not mistaken the mind of the LORD

outliers.note: He states what the alternative was: the purgation ended only on the sixteenth of Nisan, so the feast had to be held in Ijar or deferred a year, which would have been fatal to the spirit of reformation then current.

themes: the passover in the second month
a proviso for individuals extended to a nation
2.pericope_label: The counsel to keep it in the second month

schools.summary: Gill supplies the third reason from the preceding chapter, the cleansing unfinished until the sixteenth.
Keil and Delitzsch refuse the numerical sense of “sufficiently” and refer the deficiency to the priesthood generally; Ellicott glosses the word literally and takes it of number.
Wesley, so far as his note is legible, stands with the numerical reading.

debates.question: What does “sufficiently” qualify?

sides.position: Number: too few priests had purified themselves in time
Not number at all, which cannot be defended, but the state of the priesthood in general
The numerical reading is the usual one, held by Rashi and the Vulgate and by Bertheau
holders: Rashi, the Vulgate and Bertheau (as reported by Keil and Delitzsch)

outliers.note: He allows that the passover might perhaps have been held even so, had the two hindrances named here not prevented it.

themes: they could not keep it at that time
the priests had not sanctified themselves sufficiently
3.pericope_label: They could not keep it at that time

schools.summary: Gill reads the assent as unanimous and the decree as a formal vote to appoint heralds.

Ellicott renders the idioms closely, notes the inversion of “from Dan to Beersheba”, and settles the disputed clause by the ancient versions; Keil and Delitzsch accept the Vulgate’s blunt “they decreed”.

debates.question: What does the clause giving the reason for the proclamation mean?

sides.position: Not in multitude had they kept it: the people had not been in the habit of coming in their numbers
They had long failed to keep it by the precepts of the law, a lapse dating from the division of the kingdom
holders: Rashi (as reported by Keil and Delitzsch)

sides.position: That their wealth had grown greatly
holders: the Syriac and Arabic (as reported, and dismissed, by Ellicott)

outliers.note: He points out that the proclamation runs from Beersheba to Dan, inverting the ancient form of the phrase to suit a summons issued from the south.

themes: not in multitude had they kept it
4.pericope_label: The thing pleased the king, and the decree went out

schools.summary: Gill marks the circuit as covering both kingdoms.

Ellicott argues from Assyrian that the word means survivors, and reads the plural “kings of Assyria” as the historian’s phrase rather than the herald’s; Keil and Delitzsch leave the couriers’ rank undetermined.
Clarke glosses the runners as men light of foot and confidential.

debates.question: What sort of men were the posts?

sides.position: It cannot be determined whether royal body-guard or other couriers
The soldiers of the body-guard seem to have acted as royal messengers
Men usually employed to carry messages, light of foot and confidential

outliers.note: He notes that the Syriac renders the word with a borrowed Latin term for letter-carriers, which the Arabic in turn misreads as “folk of Tiberias”.

themes: the posts went with the letters
6.pericope_label: The posts go with the letters: turn again unto the LORD

schools.summary: Gill names the trespass as calf-worship and neglect of the temple, with the Targum’s milder phrasing.
Ellicott dates the fathers’ guilt from Jeroboam and identifies the brethren as Naphtali and the Trans-Jordan; he also judges the whole address a literary composition.
Henry turns the stiff neck inward, as a thing bred in the bone.

debates.question: What does “yield yourselves” translate?

sides.position: Submission, as in the giving of the hand at Solomon’s accession
Not submission here: the preposition differs, and the idiom means giving the hand as a pledge of fidelity
Consent to take him for your God — a bargain confirmed by giving the hand

outliers.note: He holds that the recurrence of these phrases in the preceding chapters proves the ideal character of the addresses, making the words the chronicler’s framing rather than a record of what was said.

themes: give the hand to the LORD
the ideal character of these addresses
7.pericope_label: Be not like your fathers; yield yourselves unto the LORD

schools.summary: Gill follows the Targum in reading the turning as a return to the fear and worship of God.
Keil and Delitzsch set the two turnings side by side; Ellicott shifts the pity onto the captives as its object and marks that the closing verb differs from the one before.
Clarke takes the promise through the Targum and finds the shechinah in it.

debates.question: What does the promise of compassion mean?

sides.position: The exiles shall find mercy from those who carried them away, and shall return to this land
They shall become objects of pity before their captors, the word denoting what inspires compassion

outliers.note: Through the Targum he makes the thing promised an abiding rather than an attitude — the LORD not causing his majesty, the shechinah, to ascend up from among them.

themes: if ye turn again unto the LORD
he will not turn away his face
9.pericope_label: Your God is gracious and merciful

schools.summary: Gill explains the freedom of the couriers from Hoshea’s character and draws the consequence that the hearers had no excuse left.
Keil and Delitzsch explain how a conquered land could still be full of cities; Ellicott reads the itinerary as a mark of historical truth and catches the continuous force of the verbs.
Wesley explains the refusal by lost appetite and dates its cost at six years.

debates.question: How could the posts travel city to city in a ruined kingdom?

sides.position: The Assyrians took the fortresses and the flower of the people only; many escaped and resettled the spared towns
The messengers in fact went no farther than Zebulun, which lends an air of historical truth to the account

outliers.note: He argues from the tribes named that the account is self-consistent, Asher lying partly next to Zebulun and the rest south of it, the Trans-Jordan and Naphtali having been devastated.

10.pericope_label: The posts mocked in Ephraim, yet some humbled themselves

schools.summary: Gill ascribes the one heart to the power and efficacy of divine grace.
Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott both note that the hand of God is normally punitive and is here a helping hand; Ellicott reads the royal order as prophetically inspired.
Henry generalises: in the day of power subjects are made willing, and God works both the willing and the doing.
Wesley marks the verse as the stated reason for a wonderful change in men lately given up to idolatry.

debates.question: What is the force of “the hand of God was upon them”?

sides.position: Normally chastisement, as in the plague on Egypt’s cattle, but here a helping hand and an influence for good

outliers.note: He takes “by the word of the LORD” as a statement of authority: the royal order was inspired through a prophet, which puts the irregular passover on firmer ground than the king’s own argument from the proviso.

themes: the hand of God upon Judah
by the word of the LORD
12.pericope_label: The hand of God in Judah, and the great congregation

schools.summary: Gill notes only that they arose before they slew and ate, and catches that the day of the month was kept though the month was not.
Keil and Delitzsch harmonise the mention of the Levites with the previous chapter by distinguishing the parties in view; Ellicott calls the same thing a verbal inaccuracy due to haste.
Henry reads the clearing of the altars as the casting out of old leaven.
Wesley has the clergy shamed by the general forwardness of the people.

debates.question: Why were the priests and Levites ashamed?

sides.position: At their own former reluctance to purify themselves from the defilement of the late reign
At the comparison: their negligence was upbraided by the forwardness of the people
The cause is not assigned; they sanctified themselves under a feeling of shame

debates.question: How is the naming of the Levites here squared with the previous chapter?

sides.position: No contradiction: that passage concerns the clergy then at Jerusalem, this a wider body
It is a verbal inaccuracy, apparently due to the writer’s desire to be brief

outliers.note: He observes that although the month in which the feast should have fallen was lost, they still kept it on the same day of the month on which it was always observed.

themes: the priests and Levites were ashamed
the fourteenth day of the second month
14.pericope_label: They took away the altars, and the priests were ashamed

schools.summary: Gill distributes the standing, priests in their place and Levites in theirs.
Keil and Delitzsch state the rule the procedure departs from; Ellicott traces the irregularity forward and finds it became the rule.
Henry holds that the Levites took over what belonged to the priests only, while reporting the contrary view.

debates.question: Whose office were the Levites performing?

sides.position: The priests’ only, which the law did not allow them
The offerers’: ordinarily every man killed his own lamb, and the Levites did it for the polluted

outliers.note: He notes that at Josiah’s passover and again after the return the Levites do this same work without its being presented as a departure, so that the precedent of Hezekiah’s passover would seem to have become the rule.

themes: the Levites killed for the unclean
an exception that became the rule
16.pericope_label: They stood in their place, and the Levites killed for the unclean

schools.summary: Gill observes that the tribes named were all of the ten, where idolatry had long prevailed.

Ellicott states the illegality plainly, takes “pardon” as atonement rather than forgiveness, and reconstructs the prayer as one sentence; Keil and Delitzsch reach the same verdict on the verse division.
Henry explains why the breach was allowed, and adds Grotius on ritual giving way to public benefit.
Clarke excuses the unclean outright as coming from countries wholly devoted to idolatry.

debates.question: Were the unclean eaters culpable?

sides.position: They were excusable, coming from countries wholly devoted to idolatry
Their failure was natural in men long estranged from the legal religion, but the eating was illegal
They were not to be forbidden, lest new converts be discouraged and sent away complaining

debates.question: Where does verse eighteen end?

sides.position: The received division is obviously incorrect, caused by the omission of the relative pronoun
It is certainly wrong: keeping it forces an inadmissible supplement and refers the prepared heart to Hezekiah

outliers.note: He passes on Grotius’s inference that ritual institutions must give way not only to a public necessity but to a public benefit.

themes: they ate the passover otherwise than it was written
18.pericope_label: They ate the passover otherwise than it was written

schools.summary: Gill preserves the reading that refers the prepared heart to Hezekiah himself.
Ellicott makes the healing the averting of bodily visitation; Keil and Delitzsch name that view, attribute it to Bertheau, and refuse it.
Henry holds that omissions in duty are sins as well as omissions of duty.
Wesley reads the healing as pardon and acceptance as if they had been clean.

debates.question: What does it mean that the LORD healed the people?

sides.position: The averting of divine wrath in the shape of disease and death, as the law threatened against defiling the sanctuary
Not that: sin is itself reckoned a spiritual disease, so the healing is of the soul or of the transgression
Pardon of the sin, and acceptance of them and their services as if they had been clean
Not only forgiveness but comfort and peace besides

outliers.note: He finds the prayer’s preference of spiritual sincerity over literal observance all the more remarkable in a writer whose principal aim is to foster reverence for external ordinance.

themes: that prepareth his heart to seek God
not according to the purification of the sanctuary
19.pericope_label: That prepareth his heart to seek God, and the LORD healed the people

schools.summary: Gill says only what the law required, that unleavened bread always followed the passover.
Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott both render the odd phrase as instruments of power or strength to the LORD; Ellicott then argues partly for the older English after all.
Henry takes the fact rather than the phrase and makes praise the work of an assembly.

debates.question: What does “with loud instruments unto the LORD” mean?

sides.position: Instruments of power to the LORD: those by which his power was ascribed and praised
Instruments of strength, those that carried the psalms ascribing strength to him
Something is still to be said for “loud”, the chronicler showing elsewhere a taste for music loud and strong

outliers.note: He corrects the tense to a continuous praising throughout the festival, and notes that the “singing” of the English stands in no Hebrew original.

themes: the Levites with strings, the priests with trumpets
instruments of strength to the LORD

schools.summary: Gill renders the speech as spoken to the heart and supplies what such words would contain.
Keil and Delitzsch, following Clericus, and Ellicott both make the commended skill musical rather than doctrinal; both also narrow “making confession” away from confession of sin.
Henry assigns the teaching office from the law and takes the word for confession in four senses at once.
Clarke makes the teaching of the knowledge of God the great work of every minister; Wesley calls it the cause of the king’s kindness.

debates.question: What were the Levites commended for?

sides.position: Teaching the people the good knowledge of God, which is the work of every minister
Not teaching but intelligent playing to the honour of the LORD, against the Latin gloss
Showing good skill in honour of the LORD in their chanting and playing, so that the king praised musicians

debates.question: What does “making confession” denote here?

sides.position: Yielding hearty thanks and acknowledging the divine goodness, though everywhere else the word means to confess guilt
Neither confession of sin nor, as Bertheau proposed, approaching with thank-offerings, but acknowledging the LORD with heart and mouth
All four at once: relation, penitence, thanksgiving and supplication

outliers.note: He notes that on such festivals the priests and Levites bore great fatigue and many privations, and so needed the encouragement the king gave.

themes: that taught the good knowledge of the LORD
they ate the feast seven days
22.pericope_label: Hezekiah spake comfortably unto the Levites

schools.summary: Gill lays out three possible senses of the verb for the giving.
Keil and Delitzsch overrule Bertheau on the purpose of the gifts; Ellicott reaches the same conclusion and remarks on the chronicler’s fondness for festal joy.
Henry notes the princes excited by the royal example and asks what a great estate is good for.
Wesley makes the gift sequential, first to God and then to the people, and weighs it against an empty exchequer.

debates.question: Were the gifts given for the second week or found to be surplus?

sides.position: They were rich gifts intended for further sacrificial feasts
holders: Bertheau (as reported by Keil and Delitzsch)

sides.position: Incorrect: they were bestowed for the week of unleavened bread and simply proved plentiful enough for another

debates.question: What does the verb for Hezekiah’s giving mean?

sides.position: He separated them from his own herds, or purchased them at his own cost, or lifted them up as heave offerings
He presented them for sacrifice as a heave offering
First to God in thanksgiving, then to the people, giving away his own right in the remains

outliers.note: He remarks that the chronicler is fond of dwelling on the joy of the ancient festivals, as though he would suggest greater whole-heartedness and magnificence to the people and princes of his own day.

themes: a thousand bullocks and seven thousand sheep
23.pericope_label: Another seven days, and the provision for them

schools.summary: Gill judges the Judean contingent the largest and explains why the clergy are counted with it.
Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott divide the congregation into the same three classes; both take the comparison with Solomon from Bertheau, whom both quote.
Clarke defines the strangers by circumcision and locates the superlative in the reunion of the tribes.

debates.question: In what respect was there not the like since Solomon?

sides.position: In length, richness of gifts, number of participants and joy, the dedication being the only comparison
In composition: the ten tribes had been separated since Solomon, and many now kept the passover for the first time

outliers.note: He corrects a confusion in Lange’s note, the word for the strangers here not being the same as the one used of Israelites who had earlier come over to Judah.

themes: the strangers out of the land of Israel
25.pericope_label: All the congregation rejoiced, and great joy in Jerusalem

schools.summary: Gill reports both readings of the opening phrase and offers a reconciliation, the Levites singing while the priests blessed.
Keil and Delitzsch call the conjunction a copyist’s gloss; Ellicott notices the characteristic omission of the sacred Name, and both read the hearing of the prayer as an inference from later history.
Henry makes the blessing both prayer and promise and turns the ascent into a descent of blessings.
Clarke matches the rising smoke to the rising prayer and closes with a doctrine of falling from grace.

debates.question: Should the text read “the priests the Levites” or “the priests and the Levites”?

sides.position: Without the conjunction: the added waw is a copyist’s gloss carried in from the earlier list
Without it: these were the Levitical priests, not irregular ministrants
Both readings stand; the Targum supplies the conjunction, and the Levites may have sung while the priests blessed

debates.question: On what ground is the prayer said to have been heard?

sides.position: On the zeal afterwards shown for the temple worship and the deliverance from Sennacherib
God said Amen to the blessing, and perhaps gave some sensible token of ratifying it

outliers.note: He closes with the sharpest doctrinal claim in the chapter: that men who draw back had real grace and trifled with it, and that to say they never had saving grace is blasphemy.

themes: the priests the Levites blessed the people
27.pericope_label: The priests blessed the people, and their voice was heard
